extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social science, political economy, and social philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for conducting and evaluating sociological, historical, and political-economy inquiry, especially the inverse-deductive (historical) method and its relation to deductive and statistical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of method vs. locality of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of investigation is applicable universally, even if many of its conclusions are only locally true; one must not expect the same conclusion to issue from varying premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the universal applicability of method with the universality of particular conclusions; when premises differ across societies or times, conclusions must be re-derived rather than assumed identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master foundational-case mastery before generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever has mastered with attainable precision the laws determining rent, profits, and wages under free competition in a state with distinct classes can determine the different laws regulating distribution in other states of cultivation and landed property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thorough understanding of a clear, foundational model as a basis for adapting theory to other, more complex social states; mastery of archetypal cases aids lawful extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of Political Ethology (national character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political Ethology, the theory of the causes which determine the type of character belonging to a people or an age, is a comprehensive and commanding branch of social science that must not be neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the study of national/collective character as central: its causes are poorly understood but substantially influence other social phenomena; omission weakens practical application of other branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as both cause and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinions, feelings, and habits of the people are results of the preceding state of society and are also causes of the state which follows; they mould laws, customs, and even the character of governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutions or policies, assess reciprocal influences between institutions and national character; account for feedback loops rather than treating character as merely passive background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate ethological considerations before practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of ethological considerations is not a defect in abstract branches, but vitiates them in practical application as branches of a comprehensive social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying abstract theory to practice, adjust conclusions for differing national/individual characters; failure to do so risks misapplication—example: English economic assumptions may not hold elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by specific experience (empirical corroboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: All deductive conclusions should be compared with results of observation—verification by specific experience—through empirical laws in history or statistics where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and collate observed facts into empirical laws to prepare for comparison with theory; treat experimental/observational evidence as essential corroboration, not an alternative route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistics to trace empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In statistics empirical laws may sometimes be traced, and tracing them forms an important part of the system of indirect observation relied on for data of the deductive science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ statistical aggregation to obtain approximate generalizations; remember these are tentative and require understanding of underlying causes before extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of indirect empirical inference (dependence on remoter causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of effects give us empirical laws of causes only so long as there is reason to think that no change has taken place in the remote causes on which the immediate causes depend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying empirical generalizations to new cases, check whether remote/underlying conditions remain comparable; failure to do so invalidates the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of understanding remoter causes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to be well acquainted with the remoter causes in order to avoid applying empirical laws to cases which differ in circumstances on which the law ultimately depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and document remote causal structures before generalizing statistical findings; use deductive knowledge to evaluate applicability of observed patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive science must supervise empirical inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductive science should 'stand sentinel' over the whole process and be constantly referred to; its sanction must be obtained for every inference drawn from specific observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let empirical observation be applied in isolation—embed empirical inferences within theoretical (deductive) frameworks to judge their soundness and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize when specific experience fails (many interacting causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many special inquiries—where many causes act simultaneously—specific experience affords nothing amounting to empirical laws; the effect of a single cause is disguised by other agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious attributing causal effects from observed instances when multiple interacting factors exist; look for average tendencies across many instances and acknowledge residual uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-instance experiments rarely verify social theory
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify a theory by experiment the circumstances must be exactly those contemplated in theory, but in social phenomena no two cases are exactly alike; thus a single experiment usually cannot confirm the theory for other cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid generalizing from isolated historical or experimental instances; recognize that verification by the very case for which the prediction was made is too late to guide practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect verification via many cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion drawn about an individual case can be indirectly verified by verification of other conclusions drawn in other individual cases from the same laws; collect multiple corroborations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test a theory's general sufficiency by its ability to explain a variety of past events; use cross-case confirmation rather than relying on single-case match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory must account for present and past to predict future
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that science renders us competent to predict the future, we must show that it would have enabled us to predict the present and the past; anything unpredictable is a residual phenomenon needing explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories by retrospective explanatory power as well as prospective prediction; unexplained phenomena should drive further data collection or theory refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve residual phenomena by searching facts or improving theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is anything we could not have predicted, this constitutes a residual phenomenon requiring further study: find circumstances that account for it or extend and improve the theory itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anomalies as signals to (a) search for overlooked causal circumstances in the case, or (b) revise theoretical premises and mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish kinds of sociological inquiry (direct vs. inverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of inquiry: (1) what effect will follow from a given cause in a presupposed state of society (direct/deductive); (2) what are the laws which determine the general circumstances themselves (inverse/historical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the method matched to the question: use deductive causal analysis for conditional effects; use inverse-deductive/historical method to discover laws producing states of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive definition of 'State of Society'
rubrics_metrics.description: A state of society is the simultaneous state of all the greater social facts: degree of culture, industry, wealth and distribution, occupations, class divisions, common beliefs, tastes, government, laws, and customs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a society, adopt a holistic view—examine multiple interrelated dimensions rather than isolated features; ensure chosen variables cover major social domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek uniformities of co-existence and succession
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist uniformities of co-existence among social phenomena and derivative laws regulating the succession from one state of society to another; discovering these is the fundamental problem of social science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for regular patterns of correlation (co-existence) and causal sequences (succession) across societies and times; treat such uniformities as hypotheses to be connected with causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for progressiveness and reciprocal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Human and social properties change from age to age because effects react on their causes; reciprocal actions produce cycles or trajectories (progress), which must be accounted for in sociological method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model feedback loops and path-dependence across generations; avoid static assumptions that ignore intergenerational transmission and cumulative change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical generalizations must connect to psychological/ethological laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations from history are empirical laws only; they must be connected with the psychological and ethological laws on which they depend to become scientific and reliable for prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require an a priori grounding in human nature or psychological laws before elevating historical patterns to predictive status; otherwise limit claims to adjacent or narrowly similar cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never introduce historical generalization without grounding in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an imperative rule never to introduce any generalization from history into the social science unless sufficient grounds can be pointed out for it in human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and document the plausible human-nature mechanisms that would produce observed historical regularities before using them to justify policy or broad theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit limits of purely a priori prediction for long historical series
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of complex successive interactions and long series of reactions, it is generally impossible to compute a priori the whole historical development from elementary laws alone; historical evidence is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine deductive reasoning with careful historical study; be skeptical of grand deterministic historical laws that lack empirical and psychological anchoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate empirical laws: Social Statics vs. Social Dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of society are of two kinds: uniformities of co-existence (Social Statics) and uniformities of succession (Social Dynamics); each requires different inferential uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statical methods to infer contemporaneous relations and dynamical methods to study progress and change; be explicit about which kind of empirical law is under consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect inference across social elements cautiously; estimate limits of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring unknown social features from known ones (as in Sociological Statics) is useful, but necessary relations are not so simple or precise that results could only have arisen from one mode of coordination; estimate limits of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring by correlation/consensus among social elements, quantify or at least qualitatively assess the plausible range of variation and alternative coordinations to avoid misleading conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specialist competence (psychology/ethology) for preparing historical materials
rubrics_metrics.description: No one but a person competently skilled in psychological and ethological laws is capable of preparing materials for historical generalization, for judging comparative importance of facts and what to observe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble interdisciplinary teams and ensure investigators possess or consult necessary expertise in human nature and behavior when designing historical-sociological analyses.
